response:
The authorship problem of The Federalist concerns a precisely bounded set of texts. Of the eighty-five essays published under the pseudonym Publius in 1787 and 1788, John Jay's five contributions were never in serious doubt, and most of the remainder could be assigned confidently to Hamilton or to Madison. The twelve disputed essays are Federalist Nos. 49 through 58, 62, and 63. These essays treat the separation of powers, the structure of the House of Representatives, and the composition of the Senate, subjects on which both men wrote with comparable command. Their shared subject matter is precisely why a reader cannot assign them by content alone.

Before any attribution could be argued, scholars had to settle the status of particular essays within the contested group. Either Federalist No. 55 was written by a single author, or it was jointly written by more than one author; the two descriptions cannot both be true, and one of them must hold. Having reviewed the documentary record, Douglass Adair determined that Federalist No. 55 was the work of a single author, which settled that question. The run of essay numbers confirms that Hamilton's list, left with Egbert Benson shortly before the 1804 duel, claimed the twelve disputed essays as his own, since that list reproduces the same numerical sequence item by item. Although that list stood on record, Madison later claimed authorship of the twelve disputed essays in his own accounting of the collaboration. The two statements cannot be harmonized, and at least one of the following must therefore be true, perhaps both: Hamilton's authorship claim for the disputed essays was mistaken, or Madison's authorship claim for the disputed essays was mistaken.

Resolving the conflict required texts of secure attribution against which the contested essays could be measured. James Madison wrote Federalist No. 10; that is, Federalist No. 10 was authored by Madison, and its argument concerning faction and the extended republic is among the most thoroughly documented compositions in the series. Essays of this kind gave investigators a stable baseline of each man's prose. Working from correspondence, publication schedules, and the circumstances under which each list was drawn up, Douglass Adair concluded that the historical evidence favored Madison's authorship of the disputed essays, and his judgment settled the tension between the rival lists on documentary grounds. Adair's conclusion, published in 1944, predates the statistical study that Frederick Mosteller and David Wallace subsequently conducted of the disputed essays, which appeared in the early 1960s.

Conducting that statistical study led Mosteller and Wallace to analyze the frequencies of common function words in the essays. Such words, including articles, prepositions, and conjunctions, recur at rates that depend on an author's habits rather than on the topic under discussion, which makes them resistant to deliberate imitation and to the influence of subject matter. Among the markers they identified, Hamilton used the word "upon" far more often than Madison did. Hamilton used the word "whilst" more frequently than Madison did. Whereas the function-word analysis supplied the raw rates for each essay, the Mosteller-Wallace study relied on neural-network classification of the essays to weigh those rates against one another and assign each text to an author.

The decisive outcome rested on the clearest of these discriminators. The near absence of "upon" from the contested texts, set beside Hamilton's heavy reliance on it, indicates the result the investigators reached: Mosteller and Wallace concluded that Madison wrote all twelve disputed essays. Their finding demonstrated that quantitative stylistic evidence could adjudicate a question that the testimony of the authors themselves had left open, and it established the Federalist case as a foundational example in the field now known as stylometry.
